UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                     BEFORE THE
                       FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

                                                           )   Docket Nos.
    El Paso Natural Gas Company, LLC                       )   CP26-558-000
                                                           )   CP82-435-000

             Joint Protest to Proposed Blanket Certificate Activity and Motion to Intervene

          The Sierra Club and Food & Water Watch (“Petitioners”) hereby protest the request filed

(the “Application”) by El Paso Natural Gas Company, L.L.C. (“EPNG” or “Applicant”) to

construct, install, modify, maintain, and operate the McCloud Lateral Project pipeline (“the

Project”) under EPNG's blanket transportation certificate issued in Docket No. CP82-435-000

(20 FERC 62,454)(“Blanket Certificate”) under §§157.205, 157.208, 157.210 and 157.211 of the

Commissions’ regulations. Petitioners request the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“the

Commission” or “FERC”) enter into a full section 7 authorization process as mandated by 18

C.F.R. §157.205(f) and seek to have this request processed as a separate application. Petitioners

further urge FERC to deny the Application under section 7 of the Natural Gas Act (15 U.S.C. §

717f) as the Project is contrary to the public interest.

          Petitioners protest the Application, as FERC approval would be premature and

inappropriate under the blanket approval process. The Project is sited in El Paso County, Texas,

a federally designated nonattainment area for both the 2015 8-hour ozone National Ambient Air

Quality Standards ("NAAQS") and PM-101. The community of Chaparral, New Mexico, a

predominantly Hispanic, low-income, unincorporated community2 just north of El Paso County

near the Texas-New Mexico border, lies in the direct proximity to the proposed pipeline route.

 EPNG's Application contains no mention of Chaparral, no environmental justice analysis, and no

assessment of the cumulative air quality impacts of the McCloud Lateral combined with Meta El

Paso data center, the proliferating data center infrastructure in the region, and other projects

including the proposed Desert Southwest pipeline.3 These omissions are fatal under FERC's

requirements for evaluating impacts on environmental justice communities.

         Petitioners further protest the Application because a full section 7 authorization process

will find the Project contrary to the public interest. Under a section 7 authorization process,

FERC must carefully weigh the costs of the Project against the benefits and develop a full

Environmental Impact Statement (“EIS”). A thorough analysis will reveal that the Project has

significant environmental and public health impacts, and that any purported benefits do not

outweigh the costs.

         This protest also serves as a motion to intervene.

    I.      Project Overview

         The Project is an approximately 5.8-mile-long, 16-inch outside diameter lateral pipeline

and a new delivery meter station with related appurtenances located in El Paso County, Texas.

The Project will be capable of delivering up to 167,000 dekatherms per day of gas from EPNG’s

South Mainline System to El Paso Electric Company (“EPEC”), with the aim of fueling a

proposed methane-fired power generation facility called El Paso Datacenter – EGUs (“the Power

Plant”) 4 that would provide electricity for, and thus enable the construction and operation of an

AI/data center called the Meta El Paso Datacenter.

     II.      FERC Must Evaluate the Project Pursuant to NGA Section 7 and NEPA

             a. The Project would have significant cumulative effects that FERC must
                evaluate

          The Project would contribute to significant cumulative effects when combined with other

past, present, and reasonably foreseeable projects in the area north of El Paso, including but not

limited to adverse impacts to air quality, noise, water, socioeconomics, and environmental

justice. FERC must evaluate those cumulative impacts pursuant to section 7 of the Natural gas

Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act (“NEPA”).

          The Project is sited in El Paso County, Texas, a federally designated nonattainment area

for both the 2015 8-hour ozone National Ambient Air Quality Standards ("NAAQS") and PM-

105. The applicant’s operational emissions projections are likely a significant underestimate

because they do not factor in routine emissions from pipeline leaks.6 Moreover, the emissions

listed in the Applicant’s Environmental Report are just the tip of the iceberg with respect to the

Project’s collective air quality impacts. It appears that the interconnected Power Plant is

projected to release roughly 3,000,000 pounds of toxic air pollutants and 26,000,000,000 pounds

of greenhouse gases every year.7 By comparison, Albuquerque and Las Cruces, New Mexico’s

two biggest cities, emit a combined total of 6.7 million metric tons (approximately

14,700,000,000 pounds) of greenhouse gases annually–about half of the Power Plant’s total.8

       The Project area already suffers from unhealthy air quality, not to mention an

increasingly hot, arid climate driven largely by the burning of fossil fuels. In its 2026 State of the

Air report, the American Lung Association ranked El Paso-Las Cruces at number 16 on a list of

the most ozone-polluted metropolitan areas in the United States, giving it an “F” grade.9 This

ranking reflects the fact that the El Paso-Las Cruces region experiences a weighted-average of

16.7 high ozone days per year. EPA has designated both El Paso and the Sunland Park area as

nonattainment areas for the 2015 NAAQS for ozone and the PM-10 limit10, and monitors

continue to report violations of the NAAQS and Particulate emission11. In addition, the

neighboring county of Doña Ana is included within the Sunland Park ozone nonattainment zone,

received an “F” from the American Lung Associations 2026 State of the Air Report12, and at the

La Union monitor, located in southern Doña Ana County, the most recent design value is 76 ppb,

a level that violates the health-based standard.13

       These elevated pollution levels cause real harm to individuals living in the entire region.

According to analysis by researchers at New York University and the American Thoracic

Society, elevated ozone levels in El Paso-Las Cruces area cause, on an annual basis, about 22

 premature deaths, 110 emergency room visits, and over 224,000 missed work or school days.14

In addition, over 1,000 Texans recently commented on the Power Plant CPCN applications15,

demonstrating wide-spread community concern over the facility.

        The Project’s water use is also likely to contribute to significant cumulative

environmental harms. This is an arid region of West Texas that suffers from drought, and any

major project like this that requires significant water withdrawals must be carefully scrutinized.

Yet the application fails to set forth a total of the Project’s anticipated water use, including from

the construction and operation of the pipeline itself, but also the power plant and data center; and

fails to discuss where that water will come from.

        These and other impacts must be evaluated when combined with other projects in the

region. The Environmental Resource Report lists a few other projects in the region, but ignores

others. It mentions the Meta Data Center and the McCloud Generation Facility, as well as the

Borderlands Expressway, a highway under construction around the City of El Paso. It fails to

evaluate the Desert Southwest pipeline (Docket No. PF26-9-000), which is a massive proposed

gas pipeline that would cross the same area as the Project in northeast El Paso, and is currently in

the FERC pre-filing process. It also fails to mention El Paso Electric’s Newman Power Station, a

285 MW gas plant located in the same area outside of El Paso, which is one of the biggest

contributors to air pollution in the El Paso region.

        In the applicant’s concise environmental report, it attempts to minimize FERC’s

obligation to evaluate cumulative effects, noting that NEPA does not contain a direct mention of

cumulative effects, and arguing: “NEPA requires an analysis of the reasonably foreseeable

effects of ‘the project at hand,’ not effects of separate projects…” Environmental Resource

Report 1, at 1-12. It then goes through several categories of potential cumulative effects and

dismisses each as minimal, with no actual analysis and flawed reasoning.

       For example, regarding Land Use and Visual Resources, the applicant first acknowledges

that “[t]he Project is in a highly urbanized area north of El Paso that is undergoing significant

Development”; but two sentences later concludes: “Given that the Project will result in minimal

permanent impacts to land use, the Project’s contributions to cumulative impacts on land use and

visual resources are expected to be minor and temporary.” Environmental Resource Report 1, at

1-17. Similarly, regarding Socioeconomics, it acknowledges that “construction will overlap or be

adjacent to other much larger projects in El Paso County”; but then summarily concludes that

“any cumulative impacts would be negligible.” Id at 1-18. And regarding Air Quality and Noise,

it claims that although other major projects will be constructed simultaneously in the area, the

impacts from the McCloud Lateral Pipeline specifically would be minimal and temporary, which

means cumulative effects would be minimal. Id.

       This flawed reasoning entirely misses the point of a cumulative impacts analysis. A

cumulative impact is “the impact on the environment which results from the incremental impact

of the action when added to other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions

regardless of what agency” reviews those other actions. El Puente v. U.S. Army Corps of Eng’rs,

100 F.4th 236, 249–50 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (quoting 40 C.F.R. § 1508.7). Without considering

cumulative effects, agencies may not realize that a proposed project would “represent the straw



                                                 6
 that breaks the back of the environmental camel.” Grand Canyon Tr. v. FAA, 290 F.3d 339, 343

(D.C. Cir. 2002) (quoting Hanly v. Kleindienst, 471 F.2d 823, 831 (2d Cir. 1972), and noting that

Hanly preceded the CEQ regulations implementing NEPA and interpreted NEPA itself). The

requirement to evaluate cumulative effects is designed to avoid a death by a thousand cuts; that

is, it is meant to address effects that can result from individually minor but collectively

significant actions taking place over a period of time.

       The applicant here argues that because the impacts of the McCloud Lateral would be

minor, the cumulative effects would be minor. However, the D.C. Circuit recently rejected that

approach with respect to FERC’s approval of a project:

       [T]he Commission said that because the project's incremental effects were insignificant,
       its cumulative effects were, too. That is a non sequitur. Again, NEPA requires the
       Commission to assess the Project's cumulative effects, which are the "effects on the
       environment that result from the incremental effects of the action when added to the
       effects of other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable actions." 40 C.F.R. §
       1508.1(g)(3) (2022) (emphasis added). Simply measuring the Project's own emissions
       against the SIL fails to satisfy that requirement. Indeed, on the Commission's view, the
       cumulative effect of a Project's emissions would never be deemed significant unless the
       Project's incremental emissions were [***17] already significant on their own. That
       approach would eviscerate the purpose behind requiring a distinct cumulative effects
       analysis in the first place, which is to account for "collectively significant" environmental
       impacts that may result from "individually minor" actions. Id.


Healthy Gulf v. FERC, 107 F.4th 1033, 1044 (D.C. Cir. 2024). The same reasoning applies here.

It is not enough to claim (without analysis) that because a project’s impacts would be minimal,

cumulative effects would be minimal. Instead, FERC must evaluate this project’s impacts

combined with other projects.

       Withdrawal of CEQ regulations regarding NEPA did not eliminate the requirement to

consider cumulative effects. That is because cumulative effects, like other kinds of effects, are

just as much “reasonably foreseeable environmental effects of the proposed agency action.” 42



                                                  7
 U.S.C. § 4332(C)(i). Cases reviewing agency actions that preceded the CEQ regulations found

that NEPA itself imposes the obligation. Kleppe v. Sierra Club, 427 U.S. 390, 410 (1976)

(stating that when multiple proposals for related actions “that will have cumulative or synergistic

environmental impact upon a region are pending concurrently before an agency, their

environmental consequences must be considered together”); Balt. Gas & Elec. Co. v. NRDC, 462

U.S. 87, 106–07 (1983) (“NEPA requires an EIS to disclose the significant health,

socioeconomic, and cumulative consequences of the environmental impact of a proposed

action.”).

        Nor did Seven County eliminate the requirement to analyze cumulative effects. Seven

County concerned indirect effects—particularly, effects “separate in time or place from the . . .

project at hand.” Seven Cnty. Infrastructure Coal. v. Eagle Cnty., Colorado, 605 U.S. 168 (2025)

. Seven County did not discuss cumulative effects—effects that are impacts of the project under

review, “result[ing] from the incremental impact of the action when added to other past, present,

and reasonably foreseeable future actions regardless of what agency” reviews those other

actions, El Puente, 100 F.4th at 249 (quoting 40 C.F.R. § 1508.7) (emphasis added). Rather than

occurring elsewhere in “time and place,” a cumulative impacts analysis provides context needed

to understand the “single project within the authority of the agency,” Seven Cnty., 605 U.S. at

190. Consequently, FERC must consider the incremental impacts of the McCloud Lateral Project

in the context of all “other past, present, and reasonably foreseeable future actions” including,

but not limited to the prosed power plant and data center, the Desert Southwest Pipeline, as well

as other already industrial facilities already in the area such as the Newman Power Plant.

             b. The Project would disproportionately impact Chaparral, an environmental
               justice community

        The environmental circumstances here demand full section 7 review rather than cursory

blanket certificate treatment. The Project is located in a federally designated ozone

nonattainment area16, and in proximity to an environmental justice community that already bears

disproportionate pollution burdens, and is within a region experiencing cumulative impacts from

multiple pipeline and data center infrastructure projects.17

        The D.C. Circuit has established that NEPA requires FERC to take a "hard look" at

environmental justice issues, ensuring that environmental justice analyses are "reasonable and

adequately explained" under the Administrative Procedure Act's arbitrary-and-capricious

standard18 and confirmed that environmental justice impacts can independently be significant

enough to require supplemental NEPA review. In City of Port Isabel v. FERC, 111 F.4th 1198 at

1209 (D.C. Cir. 2024), the court held that "effects on environmental justice communities are

certainly 'impacts' that are 'relevant to environmental concerns'" and that "environmental justice

analyses and impacts can be sufficiently meaningful to require a supplement on their own. "See

also Vecinos para el Bienestar de la Comunidad Costera v. FERC, 6 F.4th 1321at 1330 (D.C.

Cir. 2021) (holding that a petitioner may challenge an agency's environmental justice analysis as

arbitrary and capricious under NEPA and the APA); El Puente v. U.S. Army Corps of Eng'rs,

 100 F.4th 236 at 251 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (agency's delineation of the area for environmental justice

analysis "must be reasonable and adequately explained").

       The community of Chaparral, a predominantly Hispanic, low-income, unincorporated

community19 just north of El Paso County near the Texas-New Mexico border, lies in the direct

area of the proposed pipeline route. In fact, the McCloud Lateral appears to traverse right along

much of the southern border of Chaparral, but just over the line in Texas. This means the

community has little say in the approval of the project, but bears the brunt of many of the

impacts. Chaparral is also facing the construction of the Desert Southwest Pipeline, as well as

other data center and power generation infrastructure proliferating throughout El Paso County,

placing additional demands on an already overburdened air quality control region. EPNG's

Application contains no analysis of these cumulative impacts. The Commission cannot approve

the McCloud Lateral in isolation without assessing the aggregate burden on Chaparral and the

nonattainment zone.

       EPNG's Application contains no mention of Chaparral, no environmental justice analysis,

and no assessment of the cumulative air quality impacts of the McCloud Lateral combined with

the proposed Power Plant, Meta El Paso datacenter, Desert Southwest pipeline20 and

proliferating data center infrastructure in the region. These omissions are fatal under FERC's

requirements for evaluating impacts on environmental justice communities.

       EPNG's Application contains no environmental justice analysis whatsoever. It does not

identify whether environmental justice communities exist in the project area, does not assess

whether impacts on such communities would be disproportionately high and adverse, and does

 not consider mitigation. Approving a project whose application contains zero environmental

            c. The Project is beyond the scope of the blanket certificate

        EPNGs blanket certificate, issued under docket CP82-435-000, was granted over four

decades ago in 1982. The Environmental Assessment for the activities authorized under the

certificate was issued on July 1, 1981. Over the last forty-four years, the environmental

landscape of western Texas has changed dramatically. The region faces rising temperatures and

increasing dryness statewide due to climate change,21 as well as unhealthy air quality, formally

recognized by an ozone nonattainment designation in 2021.22 Further, when the certificate was

granted in 1982, AI/data centers were no more than science fiction. As neither the baseline

environment conditions, nor the Project’s specific purpose, scope, or impacts, were considered

when FERC issued the blanket certificate, it would be inappropriate to authorize the Project

under the certificate. Instead, the Commission must engage in a full section 7 process.

            d. The Project is contrary to the public interest

        Under section 7 of the Natural Gas Act (“NGA”), FERC may approve a project if it “is or

will be required by the present or future public convenience and necessity.” 15 U.S.C. § 717f(e).

Further, FERC may “issue a certificate of public convenience and necessity only if a project’s

public benefits (such as meeting unserved market demand) outweigh its adverse effects (such as

deleterious environmental impact on the surrounding community).” City of Oberlin, Ohio v.

  Extreme Weather in Texas, Texas 2036, https://texas2036.org/weather/ (last visited Sept. 29, 2026).
22
  El Paso: Current Attainment Status, Texas Commission on Environmental Quality.,
https://www.tceq.texas.gov/airquality/sip/elp/elp-status (last visited Sept. 29, 2026). See also Texas

                                                   11
 FERC, 937 F.3d 599, 602 (D.C. Cir. 2019) (citing Certification of New Interstate Natural Gas

Pipeline Facilities, 90 FERC ¶ 61,128, 61,396 (Feb. 9, 2000)); see also Sierra Club v. FERC,

867 F.3d 1357, 1379 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (“Sabal Trail”) (“If FERC finds market need, it will then

proceed to balance the benefits and harms of the project, and will grant the certificate if the

former outweigh the latter.”).

       FERC requires accurate, complete, and updated information regarding the Project in

order to rationally weigh the Project’s harms and benefits. The National Environmental Policy

Act (“NEPA”) requires that FERC conduct an environmental review as part of this information

gathering and analysis. NEPA requires federal agencies to prepare an EIS before undertaking any

major federal action that significantly affects the environment. 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C). FERC’s

regulations require that the Commission prepare at least an Environmental Assessment for

pipeline authorizations under section 7, except when the facility falls into a categorical exclusion

under 18 C.F.R. § 380.4, is an auxiliary installation or replacement facility under 18 C.F.R. §

2.55, or requires an EIS pursuant to § 380.6(a)(3) because it is a “[m]ajor pipeline construction

project[]…using rights-of-way in which there is no existing natural gas pipeline.” 18 C.F.R. §

380.5(b)(1). As explained above, the Project should not qualify for blanket certificate review

under 18 CFR 157.203. No other § 380.4 categorical exclusion applies here, nor does the Project

fall under § 2.55. The Project is a major construction project using new rights of way, and would

cause significant cumulative effects when combined with other projects in the region. As such, it

requires an EIS under § 380.6(a)(3).

           e. A FERC NEPA analysis must go beyond the scope of the Applicant’s
              Environmental Report

       NEPA review of pipeline projects serves to ensure that the substantive decisions the

NGA charges FERC with making are fully informed. See, e.g., Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc. v.

                                                 12
 Morton, 458 F.2d 827, 837 (D.C. Cir. 1972) (“NEPA was intended to provide a basis for

consideration and choice by the decisionmakers in the legislative as well as the executive

branch”); Seven Cnty., 605 U.S. at 173 (the primary “goal” of NEPA review is “to inform agency

decisionmaking”). An agency always must consider at least “those effects” that “are relevant to

the agency’s decisionmaking process.” Id. at 187. FERC’s NEPA analysis must include–at a

minimum–a project’s environmental harms so that they can be balanced against the project’s

benefits, whether and how those harms can be mitigated, and what alternatives exist to the

project as proposed that could serve the NGA’s aims. See NJ Conservation Found. v. FERC, 111

F.4th 42, 56-57; 63 (D.C. Cir. 2024).

       NEPA requires that federal agencies must “ensure the professional integrity, including

scientific integrity, of the discussion and analysis in an environmental document” and “make use

of reliable data and resources in carrying out this Act.” 42 U.S.C. § 4332(D), (E). Consequently,

FERC cannot merely accept the information an applicant has submitted at face value, but must

independently evaluate the information, gather or request more information as needed, and make

an independent determination regarding a project’s likely impacts, how those impacts compare to

the impacts of alternatives that are currently reasonable, and which mitigation measures must be

required to be imposed as conditions on any new certificate.

       Most prominently, any adequate EIS must include the interconnected environmental

impacts of the Project, the Power Plant, and the Meta El Paso AI/data center. NEPA requires that

interrelated projects be evaluated together when neither project has independent utility. Most

recent cases about improper segmentation of projects rely on the Council on Environmental

Quality’s (“CEQ’s”) since-revoked regulations about connected actions. However, the legal

principle that a project cannot be separated into smaller segments that lack independent utility



                                                13
 merely to evade collective NEPA review predates CEQ’s regulations and derives from the statute

itself. See Swain v. Brinegar, 542 F.2d 364, 370 (7th Cir. 1976) (applying independent utility test

to determine that an EIS was required for the entire 42-mile freeway, not just a 15-mile

segment); Alpine Lakes Prot. Soc. v. Schlapfer, 518 F.2d 1089, 1090 (9th Cir. 1975)

(“Characterizing any piecemeal development of a project as ‘insignificant’ merits close scrutiny

to prevent the policies of NEPA from being nibbled away by multiple increments, no one of

which may in and of itself be important enough to compel preparation of a full EIS.”); Cady v.

Morton, 527 F.2d 786, 794 & n.7 (9th Cir. 1975) (collecting cases applying independent utility

test to determine if projects had been improperly segmented under NEPA).

       Here, the sole purpose of the Project is to fuel the Power Plant. The Project would have

no benefit without the Power Plant, and the Power Plant will not function without the Project.

Further, the construction of each is contiguous in time and place. See Seven Cnty., 605 U.S. at

190. In other words, there is no break in the chain of “proximate causation between the project at

hand and the environmental effects of the separate project.” Id. at 187. The same interdependent

relationship is present between the Power Plant and the AI/data center itself – as currently

planned, one would have no function or purpose without the other. While FERC does not

exercise direct regulatory authority over the construction of the Power Plant or the AI/data

center, at the very least, “NEPA mandates that an agency consult with other agencies [that

exercise jurisdiction] as appropriate. 42 U.S.C. § 4332(2)(C).” Id. at 188. (internal quotations

omitted). As each of these project segments are entirely dependent on–and being built for the

purpose of enabling–one-another, conducting an artificially divided environmental analysis

would result in the efficacy of any NEPA review being “nibbled away.”




                                                14
            In order to satisfy NEPA’s requirements and properly inform the Commission’s decision-

making, FERC must generate a comprehensive EIS, including, but not limited to:

               •   Impacts on listed species and migratory birds;

               •   Impacts on air quality and greenhouse gas emissions, including from line pigging

                   and equipment leaks;

               •   Impacts on area water resources, including from water use during testing and

                   routine operations;

               •   Impact on area noise pollution;

               •   Impacts due to use of Horizontal Directional Drilling, including risk of frac-outs;

               •   Connected and/or cumulative impacts of the Project, the Power Plant, and the

                   Meta El Paso datacenter as a whole (including, but not limited to, impacts on

                   species, migratory birds, air quality, greenhouse gas emissions, water, and noise)

                   combined with other projects in the region; and

               •   Project alternatives, including a no action alternative, route alternatives, and the

                   use of renewable energy sources to power the Meta El Paso datacenter.

               f. An adequate review will demonstrate that the Project’s benefits do not
                  outweigh the significant costs.

           Even a cursory assessment of the Project’s significant environmental impacts suggest that

its purported benefits do not outweigh its costs

           To counterbalance these significant human and environmental harms, the proposed

Project offers to supply gas to a singular corporate client.23 The Project's market need rests

entirely on a single shipper holding a four-year firm transportation contract for a planned new



23
     Application at 4.

                                                     15
 power generation facility yet to be approved by the TPUC. If the downstream facility does not

proceed, the Project would be a pipeline to nowhere, and a single four-year contract does not

demonstrate the kind of durable market need that justifies the environmental costs of

constructing new pipeline infrastructure in a nonattainment area. More broadly, the scope of the

benefits that FERC considers must be consistent with the scope of the costs. As set forth above,

we urge FERC to include an evaluation of the full range of impacts of the connected Power Plant

and the Meta El Paso datacenter. However, if FERC declines to consider those costs, it must also

exclude any purported public benefit associated with the Power Plant and the Meta El Paso

Datacenter. Ultimately, given the extreme imbalance between the Project’s severe harms and

minimal benefits, if that, FERC must reject the Project under a section 7 analysis.
